back: Plan Financial Management; Estimate Costs; Develop Budget; Monitor and Control Finances.
Defines how revenues and expenses will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored and controlled. Output: financial management plan. Older name: Plan Cost Management.
Developing an approximation of the cost of resources needed to complete the work. Outputs: cost estimates and basis of estimates.
Aggregating the estimated costs of activities or work packages to establish an authorized cost baseline. Older name: Determine Budget.
Monitoring financial status, updating finances and managing changes to the cost baseline. Older name: Control Costs.
The approved, time-phased project budget, excluding management reserve. Changed only through formal change control.
Cost estimates (work packages, control accounts) + contingency reserve.
Cost baseline + management reserve.
Money or time for identified risks with planned responses (known-unknowns). Part of the cost baseline. Usually controlled by the project manager.
Money or time set aside by management for unforeseen work within scope (unknown-unknowns). Not part of the cost baseline.
An early estimate with a wide range, typically −25% to +75%.
A detailed estimate made when the work is well defined, typically −5% to +10%.
Supporting documentation showing how an estimate was developed: assumptions, constraints, range and confidence level.
Summing cost estimates by work package, then control account, then for the entire project, following the WBS.
The total and periodic funding needed, derived from the cost baseline. Total funds = cost baseline + management reserve.
Comparing planned spending with funding limits. If spending exceeds a limit, work is rescheduled to level out the rate of spending.
The sum of all budgets established for the work to be performed.
Evaluating the risk remaining on the project against the schedule and budget reserve, to judge whether the reserve is sufficient.
All costs over the life of the product for preventing nonconformance, appraising conformance and failing to meet requirements.
Money spent to avoid failures: prevention costs (training, documenting processes) and appraisal costs (testing, inspections).
Money spent because of failures: internal failure (rework, scrap) and external failure (warranty work, liabilities, lost business).
Internal: failures found by the project before delivery. External: failures found by the customer.
Direct: charged to this project only (team wages, materials). Indirect: overhead shared by several projects (rent, utilities).
Fixed: does not change with the amount of work (rental, license). Variable: changes with the amount of work (materials, hourly labor).
Money already spent that cannot be recovered. It should not influence the decision to continue a project.
CapEx: money invested in physical assets such as buildings and equipment. OpEx: ongoing costs of running the business, such as wages and rent.
The cost of the result over its whole life, including using, maintaining and supporting it after the project.

front: Payback period: is shorter or longer better?
back: Shorter. It is the time needed to earn back the investment.

front: ROI, NPV, IRR: is higher or lower better?
back: Higher. A positive NPV means the project is worthwhile.
A financial analysis that compares the benefits of a project or alternative against its costs.
The range of an estimate is wide early in the project and narrows as scope and information improve, so less contingency is needed for estimating uncertainty.

front: When are analogous and parametric models reliable?
back: When the historical information is accurate, the parameters are readily quantifiable, and the model is scalable.
